uncited: Standard Solid Primitives provide exact, closed-form Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for canonical geometric shapes, enabling efficient distance-field ray marching without explicit mesh tessellation [890-signed-distance-field-sdf-primitive-definition.md].

Unlike [Distance to Natural Quadrics](1559-distance-to-natural-quadrics.md), which focuses on the algebraic derivation of quadric surfaces, this family emphasizes the practical implementation of exact distance bounds for spheres, boxes, tori, and their combinations, guaranteeing that sphere tracing steps do not overshoot surfaces [890-signed-distance-field-sdf-primitive-definition.md].

The family operates on the principle that a scene is defined by a scalar field $f(\mathbf{p})$ where the zero-level set $f(\mathbf{p}) = 0$ represents the surface [7277-implicit-surface-representation.md].

For sphere tracing to be valid, the function must satisfy the Lipschitz condition with constant 1, ensuring $|f(\mathbf{p}_1) - f(\mathbf{p}_2)| \le \|\mathbf{p}_1 - \mathbf{p}_2\|$ [890-signed-distance-field-sdf-primitive-definition.md].

This guarantees that the value $f(\mathbf{p})$ is a safe lower bound on the distance to the surface, allowing the ray marcher to step forward by exactly $f(\mathbf{p})$ without tunneling [890-signed-distance-field-sdf-primitive-definition.md].

Transformations are applied by mapping the query point $\mathbf{p}$ into the local coordinate space of the primitive using the inverse transformation matrix $M^{-1}$ before evaluation [890-signed-distance-field-sdf-primitive-definition.md].
